pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: - The balance sheet is repaired, but by one-off proceeds: gross debt at carrying value fell to USD 623.1 million and net debt to USD 75.9 million at 30 September 2026, against USD 1,122.8 million of net debt at the end of 2025, because four facilities were sold for about USD 2.2 billion. Lower debt cuts interest and refinancing risk, while the repair cannot be repeated without selling more owned assets. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M02; calculation M03

- Leverage and cover are now comfortable on adjusted earnings: gross debt is 1.45x trailing adjusted EBITDA of USD 429.8 million and that earnings figure covers cash interest 5.10x, against 3.37x reported leverage and 5.03x cover at the end of 2025. The adjusted figure is built partly from a house-adjusted fiscal 2025 number, and the issuer's own net leverage claim below zero cannot be reproduced, so the ratios are estimates rather than settled facts. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M04; calculation M05

- Cash conversion is the weakest part of the financial profile: free cash flow was USD 54.0 million in fiscal 2025 on adjusted EBITDA of USD 365.6 million and an outflow of USD 397.7 million over the last twelve months because USD 518.7 million of tax on the sale gains was paid. Thin conversion means debt service depends on EBITDA rather than on retained cash flow, so lower occupancy would reach liquidity quickly. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M06

- Customer concentration is the dominant business risk: federal agencies were 54% of 2025 revenue and ICE alone 35%, and every ICE contract can be ended for convenience or non-appropriation. Revenue visibility is therefore political rather than contractual, and the federal buyer of the four facilities now also owns the assets behind the management contracts. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M07

- Liquidity and the maturity wall are favourable: cash of USD 547.2 million and USD 551.5 million undrawn on the revolver are about USD 1,098.7 million, while scheduled principal is below USD 10.0 million a year until USD 508.0 million falls due in 2029. This makes a refinancing squeeze unlikely before 2029 unless the cushion is spent. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M01

- Capital allocation is the main creditor-adverse risk: a USD 500.0 million accelerated repurchase was paid in August 2026, the authorization was raised by USD 500.0 million twice and USD 755.8 million remained available after the November increase. Repurchases compete with repaying the 2029 notes, and the executed covenant documents that limit them were not supplied. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M08

runs.text: - Strength: balance sheet repair. Net debt of USD 75.9 million against USD 1,122.8 million at the end of 2025 follows the sale of four facilities and repayment of USD 716.3 million of debt; this reduces interest and removes the 2027 maturity, so default risk before 2029 is low unless the cash is distributed. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M02; calculation M03

- Strength: liquidity. Cash of USD 547.2 million and USD 551.5 million undrawn on the revolver give about USD 1,098.7 million against scheduled principal below USD 10.0 million a year until 2029, so a squeeze is unlikely. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M01

- Strength: demand and occupancy. Occupancy of 84.0% and the new Appleton contract expected to add about USD 75.0 million of annual revenue support earnings as idle capacity is activated. Basis: EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 7

- Weakness: customer concentration. Federal agencies were 54% of 2025 revenue and ICE terminates for convenience, so a policy change reaches revenue directly and the buyer of the sold assets is the same counterparty. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M07

- Weakness: thin cash conversion. Free cash flow was USD 54.0 million in fiscal 2025 and an outflow of USD 397.7 million for the last twelve months, so debt service relies on EBITDA and liquidity rather than retained cash. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M06

- Weakness: shareholder-friendly capital allocation. USD 500.0 million repurchased in August and USD 755.8 million of authorization left after the November increase can consume the cushion, and the limits were not supplied. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M08

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: Four detention facilities were sold to the United States through the Department of Homeland Security in two pairs: California City and Otay Mesa on 2 July 2026 and Appleton and Midwest on 4 August 2026, for gross proceeds of about USD 2.2 billion and a gain of USD 1,770.7 million. CoreCivic continues to manage them under ICE contracts expected to be modified, and the company says its discussions with ICE about buying further facilities are preliminary. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 54; calculation B03

The proceeds repaid USD 716.3 million of debt: the revolver, the Incremental Term Loan, the Initial Term Loan and the 4.75% senior notes due 2027, which were redeemed at a make-whole price on 12 August 2026. The only debt left is the 8.25% senior notes due 2029 and the Kansas mortgage note; the only new term debt in 2026 was the USD 100.0 million Incremental Term Loan of 10 April 2026. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 18; calculation B02

A USD 500.0 million accelerated repurchase agreement was paid on 10 August 2026, with final settlement expected before the end of the second quarter of 2027, and CoreCivic acquired Clinical Solutions Pharmacy on 1 April 2026 for an estimated USD 199.6 million including an earn-out. Basis: EX99.1_2026-06-30_cxw_d118761dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 75

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Year-end leverage was high and stable before the sales: gross debt was 3.55x, 3.29x and 3.37x reported EBITDA at the end of 2023, 2024 and 2025, and net debt was 3.10x at the end of 2025. In the third quarter of 2026 the sale proceeds repaid the revolver, both term loans and the 4.75% notes due 2027, leaving the 8.25% notes due 2029 and the Kansas mortgage note, which is why gross debt is now 1.45x adjusted earnings. The mechanism that matters to creditors is that the claim is smaller and longer-dated but backed by fewer owned facilities: property and equipment fell from USD 2,132.2 million to USD 1,822.8 million while CoreCivic continues to run the sold facilities under existing federal contracts. The consequence is better leverage and cover with weaker asset backing and a concentration on one federal customer, and the supplied documents do not commit the remaining proceeds to debt reduction rather than buybacks.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Cash conversion was weak even before the sales. Fiscal 2025 operating cash flow was USD 194.6 million against reported EBITDA of USD 362.1 million because receivables and other assets absorbed USD 145.0 million. For the nine months to September 2026 operating cash flow was an outflow of USD 266.6 million because USD 518.7 million of income tax was paid, primarily on the gain on the sale of the four facilities, while the proceeds arrived in investing cash flow as USD 2,113.4 million of net proceeds from asset sales. Financing outflows of USD 1,166.3 million included USD 561.1 million of share repurchases, so the cash balance rose to USD 547.2 million from USD 97.9 million, and the next move in net debt depends on further buybacks against future operating cash flow.

fields.value: Liquidity at 30 September 2026 was USD 547.2 million of cash plus USD 551.5 million undrawn on the revolver after USD 23.5 million of letters of credit. Scheduled principal is small until 2029: USD 1.6 million for the rest of 2026, USD 6.9 million in 2027 and USD 7.4 million in 2028, then USD 508.0 million in 2029 when the 8.25% notes fall due. The credit agreement allows unlimited restricted payments only while its secured leverage ratio is at or below 1.50x and the notes indenture only while its total leverage ratio is at or below 2.00x. Adjusted gross debt of 1.45x earnings is below both levels but is not either covenant measure, and covenant headroom cannot be calculated because the covenant definitions were not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Five definition points limit how the figures can be used. The issuer reports net leverage of negative 0.1x at 30 September 2026 without a definition, while carrying-value debt exceeds cash on the balance sheet; the figure is consistent with leaving out the Kansas notes, which sit in an unrestricted subsidiary, but the issuer does not say so. Reported EBITDA is the primary denominator under the method, but the sale gain makes the trailing figure meaningless, so adjusted ratios are shown beside it and are labelled as built from a house-adjusted fiscal 2025 figure. The earlier source readiness note called USD 629.6 million total debt; that is principal, and the carrying value used here is USD 623.1 million. Gross interest is printed only to one decimal in millions for the full years, so fiscal EBITDA is exact to about USD 0.05 million. Segments changed in the second quarter of 2026 and fiscal 2025 has not been recast.

fields.value: Events after the balance sheet date are few. None is in the period figures. The sale of the four facilities, the repayments and the repurchase payment all fall inside the third quarter and are in the September balance sheet. Deferred revenue is small at USD 6.0 million, so there is no material non-debt funding float; accounts payable and accrued expenses rose to USD 497.5 million from USD 353.2 million, an increase the balance sheet does not explain and that is not tied here to any funding source.

fields.value: This module sets out the business, ownership, transactions and governance of CoreCivic, Inc. (issuer cxw-1070985, NYSE: CXW) as of 2026-11-18 for the credit snapshot pathway. Scope: what the company does, who owns and controls it, what changed in 2026 and what that means for creditors. It builds on the Source readiness output supplied to it.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Creditors are now lending to a government contractor that has sold four owned facilities to its largest customer and repaid most of its debt, so credit quality rests on federal contract renewals and on how shareholder returns are balanced against that cushion.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Federal agencies produced 54% of 2025 revenue and ICE alone 35%, and ICE can end any contract for convenience or lack of appropriation. The four sold facilities remain under contracts that the company expects to modify, and two of them expire in August 2027. A new chief executive took over on 24 September 2026, and the board has twice raised the repurchase authorization, by USD 500.0 million each time.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Federal demand is the credit: federal agencies were 54% of 2025 revenue, up from 51% in 2024, and ICE alone was 35%, so occupancy, contract renewal and appropriations at one customer family drive cash flow. Every ICE contract can be ended for convenience or non-appropriation, which turns a strong 2026 into a revenue stream that depends on continued political demand rather than on contract protection.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Selling the four facilities to the federal government turned owned collateral into cash but left CoreCivic operating the sites for the buyer: gross proceeds were about USD 2.2 billion, USD 716.3 million of debt was repaid, and two of the four management contracts expire in August 2027. Lower debt improves solvency, while weaker asset backing and a customer that now owns the real estate reduce bargaining power at renewal.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 54; calculation B02; calculation B03

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Capital allocation has moved from debt repayment to shareholder returns within weeks: a USD 500.0 million accelerated repurchase was paid on 10 August 2026, and the board added USD 500.0 million to the authorization on 4 August and again on 3 November, for a total of USD 1,700.0 million. Whether creditors keep the post-sale cushion depends on covenant limits that the supplied documents describe but do not define.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Operating momentum is real: occupancy was 84.0% in the third quarter of 2026 against 76.7% a year earlier, four idle facilities were activated since early 2025, and a new five-year contract for the Appleton facility is expected to add about USD 75.0 million of annual revenue when fully activated. This supports earnings but the activation costs and the idle capacity still held are a drag until demand fills them.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Governance is adequate for monitoring but incomplete for control: audited statements, an internal control opinion and quarterly reconciliations are available, the chief executive changed on 24 September 2026 after health-related resignation, and ownership concentration, board composition and related-party dealings are not established because the proxy statement was not supplied. The sponsor and governance risk level is Medium.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The strongest evidence against concern is the balance sheet: carrying-value debt fell below cash plus undrawn revolver, the only maturity of size is the 8.25% notes due in 2029, and ICE demand is strong, with occupancy up and a new five-year contract awarded in August 2026. The view would improve if the revised contracts for the sold facilities keep current economics, if two of them renew before August 2027, and if sale proceeds keep going to debt reduction rather than repurchases. It would worsen if ICE terminated or re-priced contracts at the sold facilities, if further repurchases or acquisitions were funded with new debt, or if federal appropriations or detention priorities shifted.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - The 2026 proxy statement was not supplied, so ownership concentration, board composition and related-party dealings are not established, which keeps the governance risk level at Medium rather than allowing a firmer view.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - The terms of the revised management contracts for the four sold facilities are not disclosed, so margin and revenue on those facilities after the change in ownership are not established, which limits the confidence of the view on asset backing.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - The executed credit agreement and notes indenture were not supplied, so whether buybacks and further asset sales are inside covenant capacity is not established, which limits how far the creditor-alignment reading of capital allocation can be pushed.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Fiscal 2025 is not recast to the new segments, so statements about segment mix rest on the third quarter of 2026 and on the earlier basis for fiscal 2025 separately.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Four detention facilities were sold to the United States through the Department of Homeland Security in two pairs: California City and Otay Mesa on 2 July 2026 and Appleton and Midwest on 4 August 2026, for gross proceeds of about USD 2.2 billion and a gain of USD 1,770.7 million. CoreCivic continues to manage them under ICE contracts expected to be modified, and the company says its discussions with ICE about buying further facilities are preliminary.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The proceeds repaid USD 716.3 million of debt: the revolver, the Incremental Term Loan, the Initial Term Loan and the 4.75% senior notes due 2027, which were redeemed at a make-whole price on 12 August 2026. The only debt left is the 8.25% senior notes due 2029 and the Kansas mortgage note; the only new term debt in 2026 was the USD 100.0 million Incremental Term Loan of 10 April 2026.

fields.value: A USD 500.0 million accelerated repurchase agreement was paid on 10 August 2026, with final settlement expected before the end of the second quarter of 2027, and CoreCivic acquired Clinical Solutions Pharmacy on 1 April 2026 for an estimated USD 199.6 million including an earn-out.

Thin conversion means debt service depends on EBITDA rather than on retained cash flow, so lower occupancy would reach liquidity quickly.

fields.value: - Customer concentration is the dominant business risk: federal agencies were 54% of 2025 revenue and ICE alone 35%, and every ICE contract can be ended for convenience or non-appropriation. Revenue visibility is therefore political rather than contractual, and the federal buyer of the four facilities now also owns the assets behind the management contracts.

fields.value: - Liquidity and the maturity wall are favourable: cash of USD 547.2 million and USD 551.5 million undrawn on the revolver are about USD 1,098.7 million, while scheduled principal is below USD 10.0 million a year until USD 508.0 million falls due in 2029. This makes a refinancing squeeze unlikely before 2029 unless the cushion is spent.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Capital allocation is the main creditor-adverse risk: a USD 500.0 million accelerated repurchase was paid in August 2026, the authorization was raised by USD 500.0 million twice and USD 755.8 million remained available after the November increase. Repurchases compete with repaying the 2029 notes, and the executed covenant documents that limit them were not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The strongest evidence against concern is the combination of near-zero net debt, large liquidity and rising federal demand: nationwide ICE detention populations rebounded from an April 2026 trough to a higher level by July 2026, the issuer's occupancy rose to 84.0% against 76.7% a year earlier, and management cites funding for ICE secured through September 2029. The view would improve if the revised contracts for the sold facilities kept current economics, if the 2029 notes were refinanced or repaid early, and if repurchases were held to operating cash flow. It would worsen if ICE populations fell again as in early 2026, if the sold facilities' contracts were re-priced or ended, or if buybacks or acquisitions were funded with new debt.

fields.value: - Trailing earnings rest partly on a house-adjusted fiscal 2025 figure because no full-year adjusted EBITDA is printed, so the leverage and cover ratios could differ by the add-backs the issuer would choose and the view of comfortable leverage is an estimate.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Overall, CoreCivic presents an adequate business profile supported by long federal relationships, high occupancy and a pharmacy and services line that diversifies revenue, but credit quality is constrained by concentration in one federal customer family and by capital returns that can absorb the cushion created by the facility sales. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: earnings are rising on activations, while free cash flow conversion is thin. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on the 8.25% notes due April 2029 and on how much of the USD 1,098.7 million of liquidity is returned to shareholders. The primary downside path is a fall in federal detention demand or a re-pricing of the sold facilities' contracts. Further analysis would require the executed credit agreement and indenture, the proxy statement, and the revised contract terms. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: federal customer concentration.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The downside is issuer-specific. The initiating condition is a repeat of early 2026, when nationwide ICE detention fell by about 10,500 individuals from a January high of about 70,800, or a contract change at the four sold facilities after the change of ownership. The first operational break is occupancy: the Residential segment margin was 22.3% in the third quarter of 2026 against 22.5% a year earlier even in a strong quarter, and margin for nine months fell to 22.8% from 24.0% when populations dipped. Because costs are largely fixed, lower occupancy cuts EBITDA faster than revenue and free cash flow, already thin, turns negative. Liquidity of about USD 1,098.7 million absorbs a long period of weak cash flow, and leverage would rise from 1.45x trailing adjusted EBITDA, with the 4.50x covenant maximum far above that level although its definition was not supplied, so resilience appears sufficient to avoid a liquidity problem before 2029 unless repurchases use the cushion. Management levers are idle-facility activation timing, capex deferral and repurchase restraint. The observable triggers are ICE population, occupancy and any change to the sold facilities' contracts.
